title: Insurance Explained
text:
Definitions
Insurance (CPI). The ABS price index for comparable home building, home contents, motor vehicle and compulsory third party (CTP) insurance policies. It measures price change, not what households spend in total. It does not include health insurance, which the ABS classifies in the Health group.
Insurance and financial services (CPI group). A broader group that also includes deposit and loan fees and other financial services. It is not the same as insurance.
Gross written premiums (APRA). Total premium revenue written by insurers. It grows with the number of policies and the value insured, as well as with prices, so it is not a measure of price inflation.
Affordability stress (Actuaries Institute). A home insurance premium above four weeks of gross household income.
Underinsurance. Cover that would not pay the full cost of rebuilding or replacing what is insured. Different from affordability stress and from having no insurance.

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text: This page gives general information. It is not legal or financial product advice and does not take your circumstances into account.

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text:
The main bodies







Body
What it does




Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA)
Australia’s financial system prudential regulator (ASIC 2026d). It supervises banks, insurers and a large part of the superannuation industry. Its primary mandate is to make sure these institutions, including general, life and private health insurers, have enough financial means to meet their obligations to customers (APRA 2026b). Its standards for insurers cover areas such as capital and risk management (APRA 2023, 2019).


Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)
Australia’s financial markets conduct regulator (ASIC 2026d). It regulates corporations, markets, financial services and consumer credit (ASIC 2026c). For insurance, its work includes licensing and claims handling, misleading conduct, unfair contract terms, product design and distribution, and the accuracy of what insurers tell customers about pricing (ASIC 2025, 2026a, 2026b, 2021b; Kirkland 2025).


Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC)
Enforces the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and other laws that promote competition and fair trading (ACCC 2026a). At the government’s request, it ran an inquiry into insurance in northern Australia from 2017 to 2020 (ACCC 2020). It then monitored insurance prices, costs and profits around the cyclone reinsurance pool, reporting from 2022 to June 2026 (ACCC 2026b).


Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA)
Hears complaints about insurance and other financial services, free of charge. It is an independent dispute resolution scheme (Moneysmart 2026).


Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation (ARPC)
A public financial corporation set up under the Terrorism and Cyclone Insurance Act 2003. It runs the cyclone reinsurance pool, which provides reinsurance for cyclone and cyclone-related flood damage to homes, small businesses and strata properties (ARPC 2026). It is not a regulator.


State and territory CTP bodies
Each state and territory runs its own CTP scheme. Some license and supervise private CTP insurers, such as the State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA) in NSW (SIRA 2026a) and the Motor Accident Insurance Commission in Queensland (MAIC 2026a). Others provide CTP through a government-owned body, such as the Transport Accident Commission in Victoria (TAC 2026a).

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text:
The main laws
Insurance Act 1973. APRA’s prudential standards for general insurers are made under this Act. One example is the capital adequacy standard, which requires general insurers to hold adequate capital against the risks of their activities (APRA 2023). The Act also sets up the Financial Claims Scheme for policyholders of general insurers that fail (Commonwealth of Australia 1973). See If something goes wrong below.
Insurance Contracts Act 1984. This Act governs insurance contracts. Section 13 states that a contract of insurance is based on the utmost good faith, a duty owed by both the insurer and the customer (Commonwealth of Australia 1984a). Under section 20B, a customer buying consumer insurance has a duty to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation to the insurer before the contract is entered into. Section 35 and the Insurance Contracts Regulations 2017 set a standard level of cover for some types of policy, including motor vehicle, home building and home contents insurance. An insurer can offer less than the standard cover only if it clearly informs the customer in writing before the contract is entered into (Commonwealth of Australia 1984b, 2017).
Corporations Act 2001. A business that provides financial services in Australia generally needs an Australian financial services (AFS) licence. Since 1 January 2022, insurers have needed a licence to handle and settle insurance claims, unless an exemption applies (ASIC 2025). Since 5 October 2021, the design and distribution obligations have required firms to design financial products to meet the needs of consumers. From the same date, add-on insurance has been subject to a deferred sales model, with a four-day pause between the sale of a main product and the sale of add-on insurance (ASIC 2021b).
ASIC Act 2001. The ASIC Act and the Corporations Act prohibit false or misleading statements and misleading or deceptive conduct in relation to financial products and services, including insurance (ASIC 2026a). The ASIC Act also contains the unfair contract terms protections (ASIC 2026b). They apply to consumer and small business insurance contracts entered into or renewed from 5 April 2021 (ASIC 2021a). A term found to be unfair is void, which means it is not binding (ASIC 2026b).
Terrorism and Cyclone Insurance Act 2003. The Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation is set up under this Act and runs the cyclone reinsurance pool (ARPC 2026).
CTP laws. CTP insurance is compulsory in every state and territory and is required to register a vehicle (SIRA 2026a). Each state and territory runs its own scheme under its own law. For example:

In NSW, insurers licensed by SIRA provide CTP under the Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017 (SIRA 2026a).
In Queensland, the Motor Accident Insurance Commission licenses and supervises CTP insurers. It was set up under the Motor Accident Insurance Act 1994 (MAIC 2026a).
In Victoria, the Transport Accident Commission, which is owned by the Victorian Government, pays for treatment and benefits for people injured in transport accidents (TAC 2026a).

How CTP premiums are set is covered under Who sets premiums.

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text:
Industry code
The Insurance Council of Australia’s General Insurance Code of Practice is an industry code. The current Code was last updated in October 2023 (Insurance Council of Australia 2026a). In October 2026 the Insurance Council submitted a revised Code to ASIC for approval. Under the revised Code, the Code’s obligations would become part of consumer insurance contracts, so customers could enforce them directly. A transition period is expected before it takes effect on new and renewed policies (Insurance Council of Australia 2026b).

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text:
Who sets premiums
Insurers set their own home and car insurance premiums. For home insurance, the ACCC’s 2020 inquiry into insurance in northern Australia describes how an insurer builds a technical premium from expected claims costs, reinsurance costs, operating costs, commissions, and a margin for profit or return on capital. The insurer then adjusts it and adds discounts, surcharges, taxes, duties and levies to reach the price a customer pays (ACCC 2020, 60–61). ASIC has said that it cannot set insurance premiums, but it can hold insurers accountable for their pricing practices (Kirkland 2025).
CTP premiums are set differently in each state and territory. For example:

In NSW, insurers file their premiums with SIRA. Filed premiums must be adequate and not excessive, and SIRA may reject a premium it considers excessive or inadequate in relation to actuarial advice and other financial information (SIRA 2026b).
In Queensland, insurers set premiums for each vehicle class every quarter, within maximum and minimum limits set by MAIC. The premium does not depend on the driver’s age or driving record, or on the vehicle’s age or location (MAIC 2026b).
In the ACT, the scheme is community rated. Motorists in each vehicle class pay the same premium, regardless of their individual circumstances and risk of being involved in an accident (ACT Treasury 2026). All premiums need approval by the MAI Commission (ACT Treasury n.d.).
In Victoria, the TAC charge is paid with vehicle registration. It depends on the type and use of the vehicle and the risk zone of the postcode where it is kept (TAC 2026b).

title: Who regulates home and car insurance in Australia?
text:
If something goes wrong
Complaints. Contact the insurer first. If that does not fix the problem, make a formal written complaint to the insurer. If the insurer does not resolve it, or does not respond within a reasonable time, you can complain to AFCA (Moneysmart 2026).
If an insurer fails. The Australian Government can activate the Financial Claims Scheme if a general insurer fails. APRA then assesses each claim and decides the amount payable. Most policyholders are covered for valid claims under $5,000. Individuals who are Australian citizens or permanent residents, and Australian small businesses, not-for-profits and family trusts, are also covered for valid claims of $5,000 and above. The scheme does not apply to life or private health insurers (APRA 2026a).

Last reviewed 5 November 2026.

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Short answer
A household is underinsured when its cover would not pay the full cost of rebuilding or replacing what it owns. It is uninsured when it has no cover at all.
APRA estimates that around one in seven households in freestanding houses are uninsured today. About half of households surveyed by the ACCC rated their home insurance as unaffordable or barely affordable.

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Four different measures

Each measure uses its own data and definition.







Term
Meaning
Typical measure




Affordability stress
Premiums are high relative to income
Premium above a set share of household income


Underinsurance
Cover is too low to pay for a full rebuild or replacement
Sum insured below estimated rebuilding cost


Non-insurance
No cover at all
Share of households or houses without a policy


Protection gap
Losses that insurance does not pay
Share of losses not covered by insurance

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
What the estimates show
Affordability stress. The Actuaries Institute estimates that 15% of Australian households, or 1.61 million, were in home insurance affordability stress in the year to March 2024, up from 12% a year earlier. It defines stress as a home insurance premium above four weeks of gross household income (Actuaries Institute 2024).
How households rate the cost. In a survey commissioned for its final insurance monitoring report, the ACCC found that around half of the households surveyed across Australia rated their home insurance as unaffordable or barely affordable, regardless of the cyclone risk they face (ACCC 2026).
Non-insurance. APRA estimates that around one in seven households in existing freestanding houses are uninsured today. The estimate excludes strata properties such as units and apartments. APRA did not count uninsured households directly. It assumed that a household is likely to go without insurance when its premium is above four weeks of household income. The estimate comes from APRA’s climate stress test, carried out with five large insurers that together write around 80% of home insurance by gross written premium (APRA 2026).
The Australia Institute estimates that in 2023, 344,523 Australian households had no home building insurance and 533,229 were underinsured, about 1 in 30 and 1 in 20 households (Thrower 2025). APRA’s estimate covers only freestanding houses and is based on an affordability threshold. The two use different data and definitions and are not directly comparable.
Projections. Under both of APRA’s climate stress scenarios, the share of uninsured households could rise to around one in four by 2050. That is about one million more households than today. By 2050, over 30% of households in regional centres and over 40% in rural areas may be uninsured. APRA states that these are stress scenarios, not forecasts (APRA 2026).

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Reported reasons
The ACCC reported hearing that households and small businesses were increasing their excesses and reducing their cover in response to high premiums (ACCC 2025).
Home building cover pays up to the sum insured on the policy. Moneysmart lists rising building costs and inflation among the common causes of underinsurance, and suggests checking cover every year (Moneysmart 2026). ABS prices for building new homes, which exclude land, rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026 (ABS 2025).

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Consequences
APRA notes that a growing protection gap can lead to greater uninsured losses for households and banks, and higher fiscal costs for governments (APRA 2026).

Last reviewed 5 November 2026.

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Short answer
Insurers estimate the expected cost of claims from each natural peril separately, such as flood, cyclone, bushfire and storm, and build it into each property’s premium according to its relative risk. In 2024–25 the average home and contents premium was almost $5,000 in north Western Australia, compared with $2,310 outside northern Australia.

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
section: How insurers price natural hazard risk
text:
How insurers price natural hazard risk
Insurers split expected claims into working claims, such as theft, glass and water damage, and natural peril claims. They generally model each peril separately, estimating how often claims occur and how much each one costs. The models for natural perils are generally developed by industry specialists or reinsurers and supplemented with insurers’ own claims data. Some insurers estimate the average annual loss for a peril across their portfolio and allocate it to policies by relative risk. Others build up the expected cost policy by policy (ACCC 2020, 62).
These models combine:

Hazard. How likely and how severe floods, bushfires, cyclones and storms are at that location.
Exposure. What is at risk: the building, its contents, and their value.
Vulnerability. How much damage a given event would cause, which depends on construction, elevation and other features.

Insurers also buy reinsurance to cover very large losses, and hold capital to pay claims after a very bad year. Insurers pass higher reinsurance costs on to consumers, and the cost of capital is part of the cost of insurance (Huang 2024).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Premiums in high-risk areas
The ACCC found that in 2024–25 the average home and contents premium was almost $5,000 a year in north Western Australia, over $3,500 in the Northern Territory and more than $3,100 in north Queensland. Outside northern Australia it was $2,310 (ACCC 2026).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Recent disaster losses
The Insurance Council of Australia reported $7.17 billion in insured losses from more than 300,000 claims across the 2022 flood events (Insurance Council of Australia 2023).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Reinsurance and the cyclone pool
The Actuaries Institute found that home insurance premium increases in the year to March 2024 were primarily a consequence of higher reinsurance costs during 2023 (Actuaries Institute 2024).
The Australian Government set up a cyclone reinsurance pool, run by the Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation, from 1 July 2022. It is backed by a $10 billion government guarantee and covers cyclone and related flood risk for home, contents, strata and small business policies (ARPC 2026).
After insurers joined the pool, the ACCC found that average home insurance premiums per $100,000 sum insured in higher cyclone risk areas fell 11% in the first year. In areas with no cyclone risk they rose 6%. Up to two years after insurers joined, premiums in higher-risk areas were 14% below pre-pool levels. Insurers are passing on the lower reinsurance rates to policyholders in higher cyclone risk areas. More insurers now recognise mitigation by policyholders, but some have yet to put a framework in place (ACCC 2026).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Climate change
Australia’s climate has warmed by 1.51 ± 0.23 °C since national records began in 1910. CSIRO and the Bureau of Meteorology report an increase in extreme fire weather and a longer fire season across large parts of the country since the 1950s. Heavy short-term rainfall events are becoming more intense (CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology 2024).
APRA’s 2026 climate stress test found that, under a scenario with higher physical risks, expected annual losses from weather-related events could rise from less than $7 billion a year in 2024 to more than $16 billion by 2050, in 2024 dollars. APRA states that this is a stress scenario, not a forecast (APRA 2026).

Last reviewed 4 November 2026.

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
Short answer
Insurance makes up 1.36% of the Consumer Price Index basket. In the year to September 2026, insurance prices rose 5.4% and added 0.07 percentage points to the 4.3% rise in the CPI.

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
How the CPI measures insurance
The CPI combines two pieces of information for each item: how much its price changed, and its weight in household spending.
Price. The insurance expenditure class covers comprehensive insurance for dwellings, home contents and motor vehicles, and compulsory third party motor vehicle insurance. Health insurance is classified in the Health group. The ABS measures price change using gross premiums, collected each month from web-scraped price quotes for a range of customer profiles. The index measures price change, not what households spend in total, and the ABS does not publish separate indexes for home and car insurance (ABS 2025).
Weight. The CPI weights insurance by the cost of the service provided by insurers, which the ABS measures as gross premiums less claims, rather than by the gross premiums households pay. The ABS updates the weights once a year, using National Accounts data, and holds them fixed between updates (ABS 2025).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
section: How much insurance adds to inflation
text:
How much insurance adds to inflation
At the December quarter 2024 reweighting, insurance accounted for 1.36% of the all-groups CPI. In the year to September 2026, it contributed 0.07 percentage points of the 4.3% annual rise. The ABS calculates and publishes this contribution figure (ABS 2026a).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
The Selected Living Cost Indexes
The ABS’s Selected Living Cost Indexes weight insurance by the gross premiums households pay, rather than the net value used in the CPI (ABS 2026b).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
Taxes on premiums
When the GST was introduced in 2000, the CPI insurance index rose about 30% in a year. The premiums households paid rose much less. At the time, the CPI valued insurance at premiums less claims, which is much smaller than the premium. The GST was charged on the full premium, so the extra tax was a far larger share of the CPI’s value than of the premium. In an ABS example, a rise in tax from 5% to 15% lifted the premium by 9.5% but the CPI’s value by 22.2% (ABS 2000).

Last reviewed 5 November 2026.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
Why this site exists
Insurance costs have become a major part of the cost-of-living debate in Australia. Useful information is published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, APRA, ASIC, the ACCC, the Reserve Bank, the Actuaries Institute and others. Each serves a different purpose, and their measures are easy to misread when combined.
The site covers the insurance most households buy for their home and car. These are home building, home contents and motor vehicle insurance, including compulsory third party (CTP) insurance. It does not cover health or life insurance. What types of insurance do households buy? explains the main types.
Insurance Explained brings these sources into one place and explains what each one measures. It helps answer four questions:

What is happening? How insurance prices, claims, risks and affordability are changing.
Why is it happening? Which explanations are supported by evidence, and how strongly.
Why does it matter? The consequences for households, insurers, policymakers and society.
What can be done? Practical steps for consumers, and options for insurers, regulators and governments.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
Academic leadership
Fei Huang is Associate Professor of Risk and Actuarial Studies at UNSW Business School, UNSW Sydney. Her research covers insurance pricing, responsible AI, algorithmic fairness, and the fairness and resilience of insurance markets under technological and climate change. She co-founded and co-leads the AI4Insurance Lab, which works on responsible AI for insurance with industry and government.

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text: This page gives general information. It is not financial product advice and does not take your circumstances into account.

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text:
Home insurance

Source: (Moneysmart 2026b, 2026d).






Type
What it covers




Home building
Repairing or replacing the house when something goes wrong. It usually also covers fixtures and other structures on the property.


Home contents
Replacing household items and belongings if they are damaged, lost or stolen.



Home building and contents cover can often be bundled into one policy. Renters do not need home building insurance, because insuring the building is the landlord’s responsibility. In strata properties such as apartments, the body corporate may be responsible for insuring the building. Owners are still responsible for insuring their own belongings. Renters can choose to take out contents insurance (Moneysmart 2026b).

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text:
Car insurance

Source: (Moneysmart 2026a).






Type
What it covers




Compulsory third party (CTP)
Injuries to people caused by your car. It does not pay for damage to cars or property.


Third party property damage
Damage your car causes to other people’s cars or property. It does not cover your own car.


Third party property, fire and theft
The same as third party property damage, plus your own car if it is stolen or damaged by fire.


Comprehensive
Damage to your car and to other people’s cars or property, even if you caused the accident. It also covers theft, fire and weather events.



CTP is the only compulsory type of car insurance. You need it to register a car, and in some states it is included in the registration cost (Moneysmart 2026a).

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text:
Life and health insurance
Life insurance pays out if you die, become seriously ill or cannot work. Moneysmart names four main types. These are life cover, total and permanent disability (TPD) insurance, trauma insurance and income protection insurance. Most super funds offer life, TPD and income protection insurance to their members (Moneysmart 2026c).
Health insurance helps manage the cost of private medical expenses not covered by Medicare (Moneysmart 2026d).

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text:
Other types
Moneysmart also covers travel, pet, mobile phone and funeral insurance (Moneysmart 2026d). Its insurance guides explain how to choose and compare each type.

title: What types of insurance do households buy?
text:
What this site covers
The ABS insurance price index covers comprehensive insurance for dwellings, home contents and motor vehicles, and compulsory third party insurance. Health insurance is in the Health group of the CPI, not in insurance (ABS 2025). The figures and explainers on this site therefore focus on home and car insurance.

Last reviewed 4 November 2026.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
Short answer
Insurance prices in Australia rose 47.0% over the five years to the September quarter 2026, compared with 24.6% for overall consumer prices.
Regulators and industry bodies report higher claims costs, large natural disaster losses and higher reinsurance costs as pressures on premiums.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
How much have premiums risen?
The ABS insurance price index rose 5.4% in the year to September 2026, against 4.3% for the all-groups CPI. Over five years, insurance prices rose 47.0% and all goods and services 24.6% (Insurance trends).
Figures for specific products come from different sources and measure different things.

Car insurance. ASIC reports that motor vehicle premiums grew by more than 42% between 2019 and 2024, and by a further 8% in the 12 months to July 2025 (ASIC 2026).
Home and contents insurance. The ACCC found that average home and contents premiums outside northern Australia rose 18% in 2023–24 (ACCC 2025), and a further 10%, to $2,310, in 2024–25 (ACCC 2026).

The ABS index tracks the price of comparable policies. Average premiums also change when people insure more valuable homes or change their cover, so the two are not directly comparable.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
What goes into a premium?
In simplified form, actuaries start from a technical premium:

Technical premium = expected claims + expenses + risk and capital loading

Expected claims depend on how often claims happen and how much each one costs. Expenses are operating costs (administration, marketing and claims handling) and commissions paid to intermediaries. The risk and capital loading covers reinsurance and a margin for profit or return on capital (ACCC 2020, 60–61).
Insurers then adjust the technical premium for competitive or market positioning, or to manage their exposure. These adjustments are not directly related to the risk of the property. Discounts, surcharges for options such as monthly payment, taxes, duties and levies are applied last, giving the price the customer pays (ACCC 2020, 60–61).

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
section: What regulators and industry bodies report
text:
What regulators and industry bodies report

Claims costs
ABS prices for new dwellings rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026, and prices for vehicle maintenance and repair rose 27.4%. Insurers told the ACCC that building material and labour cost inflation is one of the factors behind high premiums (ACCC 2025). The ACCC’s final report found that claims cost inflation and extreme weather events are pushing premiums higher across Australia (ACCC 2026).


Natural disasters
The Insurance Council of Australia reported $7.17 billion in insured losses from more than 300,000 claims across the 2022 flood events (Insurance Council of Australia 2023). See How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?


Reinsurance
The Actuaries Institute found that home insurance premium increases in the year to March 2024 were primarily a consequence of higher reinsurance costs during 2023 (Actuaries Institute 2024).
After insurers joined the government-backed cyclone reinsurance pool, the ACCC found that average home insurance premiums per $100,000 sum insured in higher cyclone risk areas fell by 11% in the first year. In areas with no cyclone risk they rose 6%. Up to two years after insurers joined, premiums in higher-risk areas were 14% below pre-pool levels. Insurers are passing on the lower reinsurance rates to policyholders in higher cyclone risk areas (ACCC 2026).


Capital, taxes and levies
Insurers must hold capital against the risk of large losses, and the cost of that capital is part of the cost of insurance. Insurers also pay expenses, commissions, taxes and levies, and often pass these costs on to policyholders (Huang 2024).


Competition and pricing strategy
ASIC found that 31% of car insurance customers who contacted their insurer about a renewal obtained a lower premium without changing their cover (ASIC 2026). Pricing that takes account of how likely a customer is to shop around, known as price optimisation, is legal in Australia (Huang 2024).


Data and risk modelling
The ACCC’s Northern Australia Insurance Inquiry found that better access to data, and more sophisticated analysis of it, has enabled insurers in northern Australia to price risk at an individual address level, not at a postcode or regional level, particularly for cyclone and flood risk. This has resulted in very large premium increases for some customers, while lower-risk customers may have seen reductions (ACCC 2020, ix). In one case, an insurer’s move to address-level cyclone pricing raised one customer’s premium by 70%, from about $3,000 to $5,000, and lowered another’s by 21%, from about $1,900 to $1,500 (ACCC 2020, 65).
AI and big data allow insurers to estimate risk in more detail, down to individual properties. This more individualised pricing can lead to higher premiums for properties with higher risk levels (Huang 2024).

ABS figures: ABS, Consumer Price Index, Australia (Data API, dataflow CPI), original series, retrieved 3 November 2026. Last reviewed 5 November 2026.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text: This page gives general information. It is not financial product advice and does not take your circumstances into account. It does not recommend any insurer or product.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Renewals
In ASIC’s research on car insurance, 67% of consumers renewed with the same insurer, and 40% neither contacted their insurer nor compared quotes. Of those who did contact their insurer, 31% obtained a lower premium without changing their cover (ASIC 2026).
ASIC found that no insurer in its review explained the key factors behind a premium in quote and renewal documents. It expects insurers to explain the main factors behind a customer’s premium and why it changed (ASIC 2026).
Moneysmart, ASIC’s consumer website, suggests checking renewal notices carefully, comparing insurers and asking questions (Moneysmart 2026a). It notes that comparing prices works best for the same type and level of cover, because the cheapest policy may not give the cover needed. Comparison websites can help, but they are businesses that may earn money from promoted links and may not cover all options (Moneysmart 2026b).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Before buying a property
The ACCC found that people buying property may not know a property is in a high-risk area and may not consider the cost of insurance (ACCC 2020, 343). It recommended that state and territory governments prompt buyers to look into insurance costs, starting with advice to obtain an insurance estimate as part of their due diligence (ACCC 2020, xxx).
Moneysmart notes that a home at high risk of flooding will cost more to insure, or flood cover may be excluded. It suggests asking an insurer, the local council or an emergency services organisation about flood mapping, historical flood records and the home’s Bushfire Attack Level (Moneysmart 2026d).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Payment method
ASIC found that paying car insurance by instalments often cost 10% to 20% more than paying annually, and that 54% of consumers either did not know this or missed it (ASIC 2026).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Excess
The excess is the amount the policyholder pays towards each claim. A higher excess usually lowers the premium and increases the amount paid when a claim is made.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Sum insured
Home building cover pays up to the sum insured on the policy. Moneysmart lists rising building costs and inflation among the common causes of underinsurance, and suggests checking cover every year (Moneysmart 2026c). ABS prices for building new homes, which exclude land, rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026 (ABS 2025).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Mitigation
The ACCC found that more insurers now recognise steps policyholders take to reduce the risk of cyclone damage, but some have yet to put a framework in place and the information they give consumers varies in clarity (ACCC 2026).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Where to get help

Free financial counselling. The National Debt Helpline offers free, confidential help from financial counsellors.
Complaints. The Australian Financial Complaints Authority is a free, independent dispute resolution service.
Information. ASIC’s Moneysmart has independent guidance on choosing and comparing insurance.


Last reviewed 5 November 2026.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
About these figures


What the insurance index measures
The CPI insurance expenditure class covers comprehensive insurance for dwellings, home contents and motor vehicles, and compulsory third party motor vehicle insurance. Health insurance is not included. The ABS classifies it in the Health group, under Medical and hospital services.1


Insurance, or insurance and financial services?
“Insurance” is an expenditure class, the lowest level at which the ABS publishes price indexes. “Insurance and financial services” is a broader CPI group that adds deposit and loan fees and other financial services. The two measure different things.


The 2000 spike
The insurance index rose by about 30% in the year to June 2000. The ABS attributed this mainly to the GST. Under the method used then, the CPI valued insurance as the net service households receive, roughly premiums less claims. Taxes on premiums are a larger share of that smaller base, so the GST moved the index by more than it moved the premiums households paid.2


Monthly and quarterly figures
Since November 2025 the ABS has published a complete monthly CPI. The quarterly CPI is the average of the three months in each quarter. This page uses ABS-published monthly annual changes for the headline figure and quarterly index numbers for long-run history.
